summary: Describes how the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP, RFC 4340) uses Service Codes, which identify the intended application or service when a connection is requested. They offer more flexibility than relying only on port numbers.

plainLanguage.summary: A Service Code is a 32-bit number that names the application a DCCP connection is for. It travels in the first and second packets of the connection, so a server can tell which of its programs should handle the connection even when several programs share the same port number.

subtitle: A 32-bit number that tells a DCCP server which application a connection request is meant for.

tldr.problem: Published port numbers are scarce, and a firewall that sees traffic on port 80 cannot tell what is really running there. Applications therefore end up sharing ports, disguising themselves, or failing to get a port at all.
tldr.mechanism: DCCP adds a 32-bit Service Code that is carried in the connection request and the reply. Each socket is associated with a Service Code, and a listening port may carry several of them, so two applications can share one port and still be told apart.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard from September 2009 and was later updated by RFC 6335. It clarifies how Service Codes relate to the DCCP port registry and gives an optional way to derive a port number from a Service Code.

today: RFC 5595 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2009. It updates RFC 4340 and was later updated by RFC 6335.

sections.title: Why DCCP Added Service Codes
sections.content:
DCCP specifies a Service Code as a 4-byte value, 32 bits, that describes the application-level service to which a client application wishes to connect. A Service Code identifies the protocol, or the standard profile, to be used at the application layer. It is not intended to specify a variant of an application or a specific variant of a protocol.

The Service Code mechanism lets an application declare the set of services associated with server port numbers, and it decouples the role of a port number in indicating a desired service from its role in demultiplexing and state management. A DCCP application identifies the requested service by the Service Code value in a DCCP-Request packet, and each application associates one or more Service Codes with each listening port.

The use of Service Codes can assist a firewall in identifying the intended service and may assist other middleboxes such as a proxy server or a network address translator. Middleboxes that want to identify the type of data a flow claims to transport should use the Service Code for this purpose. When consistently used, the Service Code gives a more specific indication of the actual service than deriving the same information from the server port value. The more flexible use of server ports also offers benefits to applications where servers need to handle very large numbers of simultaneous-open ports to the same service. RFC 4340 omits a description of the motivation behind Service Codes and does not properly describe how Well Known and Registered server ports relate to them, and this document exists to clarify these issues. RFC 4340 also states that Service Codes are not intended to be DCCP-specific, so Service Codes or similar concepts may be useful to other IETF transport protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The Service Code names the application, not the port. That lets a router or firewall see what a connection claims to be, and it lets several applications share one port number without being confused for each other.

sections.title: The Problem with Published Ports
sections.content:
Most current Internet transport protocols, including TCP, UDP, SCTP and UDP-Lite, use published port numbers from the Well Known or Registered number spaces. These 16-bit values indicate the application service associated with a connection or message. The server port must be known to the client to allow a connection to be established, which may be achieved using out-of-band signalling, but more commonly a published port is allocated to a particular protocol or application: HTTP commonly uses port 80 and SMTP commonly uses port 25. Making a port published involves registration with IANA, which includes defining a service by a unique keyword and reserving a port number from a fixed pool.

In the earliest draft of DCCP, the authors wanted to address the problem of published ports in a future-proof manner, because the method suffers from several problems. The port space is not large enough for ports to be easily allocated in an unregulated manner, so many applications operate using unregistered ports and may collide with other applications. The use of port-based firewalls encourages application writers to disguise one application as another to bypass firewall filter rules, which motivates firewall writers to use deep packet inspection. And ISPs often deploy transparent proxies, primarily to improve performance and reduce costs, so that TCP requests destined for TCP port 80 are often redirected to a web proxy.

These issues are coupled: when applications collide on the same published but unregistered port, network security equipment cannot tell them apart. The designers of DCCP reasoned that a 32-bit server port space would be large enough for very simple allocation policies, but overhead considerations made a 32-bit port value undesirable because DCCP needed to be useful for low-rate applications. The solution was a 32-bit Service Code included only in the DCCP-Request packet, which requires no additional overhead for the actual data flow and still gives end systems and stateful middleboxes information about the applications in use. An earlier design in which the client used a 32-bit identifier and the server listened on a socket bound only to a Service Code was unambiguous, but it prevented two servers for the same service running on one machine, and it differed enough from existing protocols to raise concerns about deployment through NATs and other middleboxes.
sections.plainLanguage: Only a small number of port numbers are set aside for well-known services, so applications collide, hide behind other ports, or get redirected by proxies. A 32-bit Service Code carried only in the handshake gives each application its own label without adding cost to the data that follows.

sections.title: Ports and Service Codes Together
sections.content:
In DCCP, packets belonging to a connection are demultiplexed based on a combination of four values: source IP address, source port, destination IP address and destination port, as in TCP. Ports provide the fundamental per-packet demultiplexing function. The UDP and TCP port number space, 0 to 65535, is split into three ranges: 0 to 1023 as Well Known or system ports, 1024 to 49151 as Registered or user ports, and 49152 to 65535 as Dynamic or private ports. DCCP supports Well Known and Registered ports, which are allocated in the DCCP IANA Port Numbers registry, and each Registered DCCP port MUST be associated with at least one pre-defined Service Code.

Applications that do not need a server port in the Well Known or Registered range SHOULD use a Dynamic server port. Clients can identify the server port for the services they want to connect to in several ways, such as by receiving an SDP record exchanged out of band, or by using DNS SRV resource records. Applications that do not use out-of-band signalling can still communicate, provided that both client and server agree on the port value, which removes the need for each registered Service Code to be allocated to an IANA-assigned server port.

A Service Code is represented in one of three forms: a decimal number, which is the canonical method, a 4-character ASCII string, or an 8-digit hexadecimal number. All standards assigned Service Codes, including all values assigned by IANA, are required to use a value that may be represented using a subset of the ASCII character set. Endpoints MUST associate a Service Code with every DCCP socket, both actively and passively opened, and the application will generally supply it. A single passive-listening port may be associated with more than one Service Code value, and the set of Service Codes could be associated with one or more server applications. In the currently defined set of packet types, the Service Code value is present only in DCCP-Request and DCCP-Response packets.
sections.plainLanguage: A connection is still found by its two addresses and two ports. The Service Code sits on top of that, telling the server which of its programs the connection is meant for. Every socket needs one, but a listening port may offer several.

sections.title: The Reserved and Invalid Values
sections.content:
A Service Code of zero is permanently reserved, representing the absence of a meaningful Service Code. It indicates that no application information was provided. RFC 4340 states that applications MAY be associated with this Service Code in the same way as other Service Code values, and that use is permitted for any server port. This document clarifies the point by adding three rules. Applications SHOULD NOT use a Service Code of zero. Application writers that need a temporary Service Code value SHOULD choose a value from the private range. And applications intended for deployment in the Internet are encouraged to use an IANA-defined Service Code; if no specific Service Code exists, they SHOULD request a new assignment from IANA.

RFC 4340 defines the Service Code value of 4294967295 in decimal, 0xFFFFFFFF, as invalid. This is provided so implementations can use a special 4-byte value to indicate that there is no valid Service Code. Implementations MUST NOT accept a DCCP-Request with this value and SHOULD NOT allow applications to bind to this Service Code value.
sections.plainLanguage: Two values are special. Zero means there is no useful Service Code, so an application should not use it. The all-ones value is invalid, and a server must refuse a request that carries it.

sections.title: Deriving a Port from a Service Code
sections.content:
Applications that use neither out-of-band signalling nor an IANA-assigned port still need the client and the server to agree on the server port value. This section describes an optional method that derives a default server port number from the Service Code, with the returned value in the Dynamic port range. The method is a short expression over the four bytes of the Service Code, with the least significant byte last, and it substitutes 0xC000 for a result of 0xFFFF. For example, the function associates the Service Code SC:fdpz with the server port 64634.

The algorithm has four stated properties. It identifies a default server port for each service. It seeks to assign different Service Codes to different ports but does not guarantee that the assignment is unique. It preserves the four lowest bits of the final bytes of the Service Code, which allows many common series of Service Codes to map to a set of adjacent port numbers, such as Foo1 and Foo2 or Fooa and Foob, though the consecutive numbering only applies to characters in the range 0-9 and A-O and P-Z, and crossing a range boundary introduces a discontinuity. And it avoids the port 0xFFFF, which is not accessible on all host platforms. Applications and higher-layer protocols that have been assigned a Service Code, or that use one from the unassigned private space, may use this method. It does not preclude other applications from using the selected server port, since DCCP servers are differentiated by the Service Code value.
sections.plainLanguage: Without any signalling, the two ends can still agree on a port: the Service Code is put through a small formula that turns it into a port number in the private range. Two different codes may end up on the same port, which is fine because the Service Code still tells them apart.

sections.title: Using a Service Code on the Wire
sections.content:
A client initiating a connection issues a DCCP-Request with a Service Code and chooses a destination server port number that is expected to be associated with the specified Service Code at the destination. A server that receives a DCCP-Request determines whether an available service matching the Service Code is supported for the specified destination server port, associates the session with the Service Code and a corresponding server, and returns a DCCP-Response. If the service is not available, the session is rejected and a DCCP-Reset packet is returned.

A client application MUST associate every DCCP connection, and hence every active socket, with a single Service Code value, and this value is used in the corresponding DCCP-Request packet. When a DCCP-Request is received and the specified destination port is not bound to a server, the host MUST reject the connection by issuing a DCCP-Reset with the reset code "Connection Refused", and MAY also use the reset code "Too Busy". When the requested destination port is bound to a server, the host MUST also verify that the server port is associated with the specified Service Code, since several Service Code values can be associated with the same server port. If the request uses a Service Code that is associated with the port, the host accepts the connection and the server returns a copy of the Service Code in the DCCP-Response packet, completing the initial handshake. If the server port is not associated with the requested Service Code, the server SHOULD reject the request by sending a DCCP-Reset packet with reset code 8, "Bad Service Code", but MAY use the reason "Connection Refused". After a connection has been accepted, the protocol control block is associated with a pair of ports, a pair of IP addresses and a single Service Code value.

The RFC also sets out the four cases that arise when two DCCP server applications passively listen on the same host. Two servers may use different Service Codes and different ports. Two servers may use the same Service Code but different ports. Two servers may use different Service Codes on the same port. And two servers attempting to use the same Service Code and bind to the same server port MUST be disallowed, since there would be no way to direct a new connection to the correct application. The RFC replaces the RFC 4340 text with a statement that an implementation SHOULD allow more than one Service Code to be associated with a passive server port, and adds that an implementation SHOULD provide a method that informs a server of the Service Code value selected by an active connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The client names the service in its first packet. The server checks that its port really offers that service, echoes the code back in its reply, and refuses the connection if the service is not there. Two programs cannot claim the same Service Code on the same port, because the server would have no way to choose between them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All IPsec modes protect the integrity of the DCCP header, which protects the Service Code field from undetected modification within the network. The IPsec Encapsulated Security Payload mode may be used to encrypt the Service Code field, hiding its value inside the network and preventing interpretation by middleboxes. The DCCP header is not protected by application-layer security such as the use of DTLS.

The RFC identifies four areas of security that matter. Server port number reuse: because Service Codes are used in addition to ports when demultiplexing incoming connections, and because the Service Code allows multiple applications to share the same port number even on the same host, server port number reuse in DCCP may be more common than in TCP and UDP. Association of applications with Service Codes: the mechanism gives more ready feedback that a concrete service is associated with a given port, because systems using it immediately confirm or deny that a particular service is present, where systems not using it may only indicate that some service is or is not available. This may have implications in terms of port scanning and reconnaissance, and the same service may be reached through more than one Service Code. Implementors also need to guard against the increased opportunities for denial-of-service attacks, since processing Service Codes implies more processing than arriving port numbers do. Interaction with IPsec: use of port numbers in IPsec selectors and firewalls may assume the numbers correspond to Well Known services, but there is no such requirement, since any service may run on any port subject to mutual agreement between the endpoint hosts. Use of the Service Code may interfere with that assumption within IPsec and within firewall systems, but it does not add a new vulnerability, and new implementations should not rely on either port numbers or Service Codes to indicate a specific service.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec protects the Service Code on the wire, so a network cannot change it unnoticed. But a server that answers differently for each Service Code gives an attacker a finer-grained way to probe it, so this can make port scanning more informative than before.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
This document does not change the IANA allocation procedures for the DCCP Port Number and DCCP Service Codes registries defined in RFC 4340. Associations of Service Codes with Well Known ports are defined in the IANA DCCP Port registry, and the set of registered Service Codes for use within the general Internet is an IANA-controlled name space. Private Service Codes are not centrally allocated and are denoted by the decimal range 1056964608 to 1073741823, that is, 32-bit values with the high-order byte equal to 63, which corresponds to the ASCII character '?'.

For completeness, the RFC notes that it is not required to supply an approved document such as a published RFC to support an application for a DCCP Service Code or port number value, although RFCs may be used to request Service Code values through the IANA Considerations section. A specification is however required to allocate a Service Code that uses a combination of ASCII digits, uppercase letters and the characters space, hyphen, dot and slash.
sections.plainLanguage: The registries stay as RFC 4340 set them up. Values in the top part of the range, from 1056964608 to 1073741823, are set aside for private use, and a published RFC is not required to get one.
